scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Expressionist dance originated in early 20th-century Europe, particularly Germany and the USA, as a protest against the formalism of classical ballet.
Isadora Duncan, dancing barefoot around 1900, was a key early figure who sought to unite body, mind, and spirit, drawing on ancient art for inspiration.
Rudolf von Laban developed theoretical frameworks and notation for the dance, teaching at Monte Verità in Switzerland.
on_screen: Map: Germany · Europe

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Expressionist dance was performed as an artistic statement and personal expression, often in solo or small group performances.
It was a form of protest against traditional ballet and societal norms, emphasizing individuality, emotion, and spiritual connection.
It also had feminist significance, with many women leading the movement.

Rhythm and expressive movement are central, with experimentation in musical accompaniment to enhance emotional impact.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Costumes are often minimal or naturalistic, reflecting the dance’s emphasis on natural movement and body expression.
Isadora Duncan famously danced barefoot and in simple tunics inspired by ancient Greek art.
The setting can vary but often includes studio or stage spaces conducive to improvisation and expressive movement.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Isadora Duncan, Rudolf von Laban, Mary Wigman, Gret Palucca, Harald Kreutzberg, Hanya Holm, Ruth St. Denis, Ted Shawn, Martha Graham, Liz Aggiss, Birgit Åkesson, Dore Hoyer, Jo Mihaly.
The movement was strongest in Germany and the USA, with schools in Dresden and the Denishawn School in the USA.
Expressionist dance evolved from late 19th-century efforts to free dance from classical constraints, influenced by the Delsarte system and early modern dancers like Loie Fuller and Isadora Duncan.

scenes.title: Family tree

expressionist dance is influence of Butoh: Japanese Butoh was inspired by German expressionist dance after WWII.
